top.title: Agentic Code Review
top.author: Addy Osmani
top.summary: AI generates code faster but creates more issues, making review the slowest and costliest part of development. Human reviewers must spend more time understanding AI-written code since it lacks clear reasoning. Teams should focus on using AI to handle simple checks and save human effort for critical reviews where mistakes matter most.

top.title: Watching for file changes on macOS
top.author: alexwlchan
top.summary: The article explains how to use macOS’s FSEvents API in Swift to watch for file changes and print the changed file paths. It shows how a Python script can read these paths from the Swift script’s output to trigger actions like rebuilding a site. This method detects file changes quickly, with just a few milliseconds delay.

top.title: Why TypeScript 7.0 Was Rewritten in Go — And What It Means for Your Dev Stack
top.author: spf13
top.summary: TypeScript 7.0 was rewritten in Go to make builds much faster and code easier to maintain. Go’s simplicity, fast compile times, and strong typing help catch errors early and support long-running, complex systems. For AI-driven development, Go is the best choice for building reliable infrastructure, while Python and Rust serve other important roles.

top.title: Agentic Autonomy Levels
top.author: Addy Osmani
top.summary: Agentic autonomy levels guide how much freedom AI agents have, balancing risk and control. Lower levels need human oversight, while higher levels let agents work independently or in parallel with evidence to verify success. The best approach matches autonomy to task risk and verification, ensuring safe and effective AI use.

top.title: Vibe Coding Is Dangerous, Agentic Engineering Isn't—Wes McKinney
top.author: Simon Späti
top.summary: Wes McKinney uses careful planning and AI agents to write and review code, avoiding "vibe coding." He builds tools that help maintain projects and improve AI-driven development. Wes believes strong specs and engineering skills are key for successful agentic engineering in the future.

top.title: Migrating from GNU stow to chezmoi
top.author: Redowan's Reflections
top.summary: The author switched from GNU stow to chezmoi to manage dotfiles without automatic symlink updates, preferring deliberate changes. Chezmoi stores real config files in a git repo and applies them to the home directory, running scripts and handling machine-specific settings. This setup simplifies bootstrapping new Macs and keeps agent skills and configs consistent across devices.

top.title: Gateway pattern to invoke external dependencies
top.author: Redowan Delowar
top.summary: The Gateway pattern helps separate business logic from external service calls by using interfaces. In Go, the consumer defines the interface, allowing easy testing with mocks. This design keeps the service and external dependencies independent and testable.

top.title: Starting Systems Programming, Pt 1: Programmers Write Programs
top.author: Efron Licht
top.summary: The article explores systems programming by examining what a program is and how to interact with its data. It includes practical exercises using Go programs and bash scripts to read, write, and manipulate binary data. The goal is to understand programming fundamentals and build tools to analyze programs effectively.

top.title: An AI agent coding skeptic tries AI agent coding, in excessive detail
top.author: Max Woolf's Blog
top.summary: The author tested AI coding agents and found them surprisingly good at writing and optimizing Rust and Python code. These agents created fast, efficient machine learning tools that rival existing libraries. The author encourages others to try modern agents with clear coding guidelines for better results.

top.title: LLMs and performative productivity
top.author: Josh Collinsworth
top.summary: AI tools like large language models (LLMs) often make developers feel more productive, but studies show they may actually slow work and reduce skill growth. Productivity gains are mostly seen in simple tasks, while complex projects can suffer from lower code quality and more maintenance. True productivity is hard to measure and requires careful thought, not just faster or more code output.

top.title: / Isometric NYC
top.author: cannoneyed.com
top.summary: The author used AI agents to help build a pixel art map of NYC with very little coding. Image generation models still struggle with mistakes and automation is hard. Despite challenges, AI tools make large creative projects possible and inspire hope for the future.

top.title: How Servers Work: A Hands-On Introduction to TCP Sockets
top.author: Ivan Velichko
top.summary: A TCP server communicates by sending and receiving data over network connections called sockets. TCP ensures reliable and ordered delivery of data between clients and servers using ports and connections. The article explains how to build a simple TCP server and client in Python using sockets to send and receive data.

top.title: Shipping at Inference-Speed
top.author: Peter Steinberger
top.summary: AI models like Codex and GPT-5.2 now write working code fast, so the author spends more time thinking than typing. He uses agents and queues to iterate quickly and prefers simple, agent-friendly codebases. Improved models reduced the need for tools he built, letting him build and refactor more often.

top.title: Software Engineering in the Age of AI
top.author: Andrew Diamond
top.summary: AI has changed software development by writing most code, while humans now mainly review and guide it. top.title: Prompt caching: 10x cheaper LLM tokens, but how?
top.author: ngrok
top.summary: Prompt caching stores and reuses parts of LLM requests to avoid repeating work. This cuts token usage and cost by up to tenfold. It requires tracking inputs, outputs, and cache validity to stay correct.

top.title: Why AI hasn’t replaced software engineers, and won’t
top.author: Arvind Narayanan

top.title: How to build a remarkable command palette

top.summary: A command palette is a user interface tool that allows quick access to various commands, making it easier for users to discover features. shortest.title: Ownership

It involves thinking deeply about the issue, testing carefully, and making sure the solution works well in production. Juniors should learn to aim for this level of care and ask for help when needed.

shortest.title: USB in a NutShell
shortest.author: beyondlogic.org
shortest.summary: The USB standard can initially seem overwhelming due to its extensive documentation, but not all sections are essential to read thoroughly. For those designing USB peripherals, focusing on specific chapters like Architectural Overview, USB Data Flow Model, USB Device Frame Work, and USB Host Hardware and Software can provide the necessary insights. Understanding the different speeds, bus topology, architecture, and controller interfaces of USB is crucial for developing devices efficiently within the USB framework. The document also touches on the benefits of USB's tiered star topology, power monitoring capabilities, support for multiple devices, and the evolution of USB host controllers to accommodate increasing bandwidth demands.

shortest.title: “Conviction Collapse” and the End of Software as We Know It

shortest.summary: Software is no longer a fixed product but a flexible process that evolves through ongoing learning and creativity. AI and agentic coding let people build, adapt, and improve software like art or music. Success now depends on play, social interaction, and discovering new ways to create, not just on money or technology.

shortest.title: The (lazy) Git UI You Didn't Know You Need

shortest.title: If you thought the speed of writing code was your problem - you have bigger problems

shortest.summary: Writing code faster does not make software delivery faster if other steps are slow. The real problem is delays in review, testing, and deployment, plus unclear requirements. To improve, fix the slowest step and focus on getting features into users' hands quickly.

shortest.title: Technical blogging lessons learned

The Rust version fixes many memory leaks and shrinks the binary size by about 20%. This rewrite makes Bun faster, smaller, and more stable with better tools for future improvements.

deep_reading.title: From Technical Debt to Cognitive and Intent Debt
deep_reading.author: arxiv.org
deep_reading.summary: Software development now faces three kinds of debt: technical debt (messy code), cognitive debt (lost shared understanding), and intent debt (unclear goals). Generative AI speeds up coding but can worsen cognitive and intent debt by reducing team understanding and clarity. To stay healthy, software teams must focus as much on clear intent and shared knowledge as on code quality.

deep_reading.title: Why Elixir is the best language for AI
deep_reading.author: José Valim
deep_reading.summary: Elixir is the best language for AI because it is easy to understand, stable, and well-documented. Its features like immutability and clear data flow help both humans and AI models reason about code. Also, Elixir’s fast feedback, low complexity, and introspection tools make coding and debugging quicker and simpler.

deep_reading.title: What Async Promised and What it Delivered
deep_reading.author: Causality
deep_reading.summary: Async programming evolved from callbacks to promises to async/await, each improving code readability but adding new challenges. Async/await makes asynchronous code look sequential, which helps for simple tasks but hides complexity in larger programs. Overall, these advances helped developers write async code easier but introduced new bugs and harder maintenance in big projects.

deep_reading.title: Why German Strings are Everywhere
deep_reading.author: cedardb.com
deep_reading.summary:
German Strings use a single 128-bit layout to represent any string.  
Strings of 12 or fewer characters are stored inline; longer strings store a length, a pointer, and a four-character prefix for fast checks.  
They are immutable and support persistent, transient, and temporary storage classes to cut copies and speed reads, but appending is costly and lifetimes must be managed.

deep_reading.title: Starting Systems Programming 03: Execution Counts: Software Performance & Measurement
deep_reading.author: eblog: software articles by efron licht
deep_reading.summary: Software performance is best improved by focusing on memory and in-process operations early in design. Benchmarks and profiling help identify bottlenecks and optimize tasks like memory allocation. Using techniques like pooling reduces runtime and memory use, saving costs and improving efficiency.

deep_reading.title: What every programmer absolutely, positively needs to know about encodings and character sets to work with text
deep_reading.author: kunststube.net
deep_reading.summary: To work with text in computers, understanding encodings and character sets is essential. Unicode is a standard that unifies different encoding schemes, like UTF-8 and UTF-16, which represent characters using varying numbers of bits. It's important to specify the encoding used for text, as incorrect handling can lead to unreadable documents.

deep_reading.title: Migrating from Go to Rust
deep_reading.author: Matthias Endler
deep_reading.summary: Go and Rust both offer strong concurrency and performance, but Rust has stricter safety checks and a more powerful type system. Rust’s generics and traits provide better code reuse and fewer runtime errors, though compile times are slower and the learning curve is steeper. Moving from Go to Rust means trading simplicity and fast builds for safety, expressiveness, and fewer runtime bugs.

The document also touches on the benefits of USB's tiered star topology, power monitoring capabilities, support for multiple devices, and the evolution of USB host controllers to accommodate increasing bandwidth demands.

deep_reading.title: Rewriting the world in Rust
deep_reading.author: John Arundel
deep_reading.summary: Rust is a modern language that improves software security by preventing many memory and concurrency bugs. Rewriting all old code in Rust is very hard, and automatic translation does not create good Rust programs. Instead, gradually replacing parts with Rust and redesigning code step-by-step is a more practical and effective approach.

deep_reading.title: Year in review: Limitless, Sesame, Claude Code, and more
deep_reading.author: paulstamatiou.com
deep_reading.summary: In 2025, Paul Stamatiou focused on designing and building simple, high-quality AI products that feel personal and useful. He left his startup role to join Sesame as Head of Design, working closely on software and hardware. He believes great design means thoughtful product building, not just flashy visuals or shortcuts with AI.

deep_reading.title: Mechanical Watch
deep_reading.author: Bartosz Ciechanowski
deep_reading.summary: A mechanical watch keeps time using a few key parts: a mainspring, gears, an escapement, and a balance wheel. The mainspring stores energy that travels through gear trains to drive the hands while the escapement and balance wheel regulate the speed. Additional mechanisms let you wind, set the time, and protect the movement from shocks.

deep_reading.title: Up the Stack: How AI’s Escape From the Commodity Trap Risks Enterprise Lock-in
deep_reading.author: Arvind Narayanan
deep_reading.summary: AI companies face challenges making profits by just selling model inference because it is a commodity with little differentiation. To succeed, they must move up the stack by offering integrated services and creating switching costs like traditional enterprise software firms. This shift raises important questions about competition, innovation, and who will benefit from AI’s economic impact.

deep_reading.title: Celebrating 50 years of Microsoft | Bill Gates
deep_reading.author: Bill Gates
deep_reading.summary: Bill Gates reflects on the 50th anniversary of Microsoft, starting with the creation of Altair BASIC in 1975. He shares his pride in how this early code led to a revolution in computing and the company's immense success. Gates also acknowledges the influential teachers who helped shape his journey into the world of technology.

deep_reading.title: Making Software: How is data stored?
deep_reading.author: makingsoftware.com
deep_reading.summary: Memory is stored using different technologies like fast but costly SRAM, capacitors in DRAM that need refreshing, and charge trap cells in SSDs arranged in 3D stacks. Each type balances speed, capacity, and cost differently to meet various needs. The ultimate goal is to create memory that is fast, dense, and long-lasting.

deep_reading.title: How Markdown took over the world
deep_reading.author: Anil Dash
deep_reading.summary: Markdown started as a simple way to make writing on the internet easier without needing complicated code. Many people liked it and began using it everywhere, from blogs to apps like Microsoft Notepad and Apple Notes. Its success shows how open, easy ideas can grow big and change how we share information online.

deep_reading.title: Twenty Five Years of Computing
deep_reading.author: susam.net
deep_reading.summary: The author has over 25 years of experience in software development, starting from university days. Early challenges and learning moments helped them grow into a skilled engineer. They value professionalism, continuous learning, and kindness in their career.

deep_reading.title: The essence of architectural work - Part 2
deep_reading.author: Blog on Uwe Friedrichsen
deep_reading.summary: Many architectural anti-patterns in software happen because people don't understand why architecture matters. These anti-patterns cause bad designs that don't fit the project's real needs. Knowing the true purpose of architectural work helps avoid these problems and leads to better software.

deep_reading.title: Hashing
deep_reading.author: Sam Rose
deep_reading.summary: Hash functions turn inputs into numbers and help organize data efficiently. Good hash functions avoid collisions and spread outputs evenly to keep systems fast. They are important for tools like hash maps and use techniques like random seeds to stay secure.

deep_reading.title: The Software Industrial Revolution
deep_reading.author: cannoneyed.com
deep_reading.summary: The Software Industrial Revolution will make software much cheaper and easier to create. This change will boost demand for software and transform many industries beyond tech. As software becomes abundant, it will drive faster innovation and reshape the global economy.

deep_reading.title: how-did-i-get-here.net
deep_reading.author: Lexi
deep_reading.summary: This site runs a traceroute to show the path your packets took across the Internet. Routers in different networks (autonomous systems) pass packets along using BGP routing. The traceroute lists those routers and ASes so you can see how reachability is determined.

deep_reading.title: Goodbye, forever, probably.
deep_reading.author: whitep4nth3r.com
deep_reading.summary: The author has retired from developer relations after years of burnout and industry changes. They no longer find value in teaching tech as the field shifts with AI and new trends. Now, they look forward to a quieter role as a staff engineer and rebuilding themselves away from the spotlight.

deep_reading.title: Technical blogging lessons learned
deep_reading.author: Cynthia Dunlop
deep_reading.summary: Writing regularly helps overcome doubts and improves skills over time. Focus on topics that interest you and your audience, even if others have written about them. Use simple tools, be honest, and don’t worry about perfection or criticism.
deep_reading.notes: В посте есть ссылки на отличные блоги (в частности, узнал отсюда про Preston Thorpe) - поэтому его надо читать внимательно и просмотреть связанные блоги.

deep_reading.title: If you thought the speed of writing code was your problem - you have bigger problems
deep_reading.author: Debugging Leadership
deep_reading.summary: Writing code faster does not make software delivery faster if other steps are slow. The real problem is delays in review, testing, and deployment, plus unclear requirements. To improve, fix the slowest step and focus on getting features into users' hands quickly.

deep_reading.title: “Conviction Collapse” and the End of Software as We Know It
deep_reading.author: Tim O’Reilly
deep_reading.summary: Software is no longer a fixed product but a flexible process that evolves through ongoing learning and creativity. AI and agentic coding let people build, adapt, and improve software like art or music. Success now depends on play, social interaction, and discovering new ways to create, not just on money or technology.

deep_reading.title: What Happened To WebAssembly
deep_reading.author: EmNudge
deep_reading.summary: WebAssembly is widely used to run code efficiently and securely in browsers and other environments, often as a compilation target for many languages. It is not replacing JavaScript but works behind the scenes to improve performance and enable new features. Its strength lies in security, portability, and embeddability rather than being a standalone language for building entire applications.

deep_reading.title: How WebSockets Work
deep_reading.author: Kaan Peksen
deep_reading.summary: WebSockets upgrade an HTTP connection to a persistent, full-duplex channel so server and client can send messages anytime. They shine for real-time apps like chat and multiplayer games but are stateful, harder to proxy and scale, and can be inefficient if you send large JSON frequently. Optimize by sending compact binary data and choose simpler options (EventSource or HTTP) when only server-to-client updates are needed.

deep_reading.title: AI vs. human illustrators? AI + human illustrators!
deep_reading.author: Travis Turner (richardturner@evilmartians.com)
deep_reading.summary: Evil Martians tried using AI alone to create blog illustrations but found many problems with quality and consistency. They now use a mix of AI and human illustrators, where AI does most work and humans finish the details. This hybrid approach saves time, lowers costs, and improves the final images.

tutorials.title: Watching for file changes on macOS
tutorials.author: alexwlchan
tutorials.summary: The article explains how to use macOS’s FSEvents API in Swift to watch for file changes and print the changed file paths. It shows how a Python script can read these paths from the Swift script’s output to trigger actions like rebuilding a site. This method detects file changes quickly, with just a few milliseconds delay.

tutorials.title: Migrating from GNU stow to chezmoi
tutorials.author: Redowan's Reflections
tutorials.summary: The author switched from GNU stow to chezmoi to manage dotfiles without automatic symlink updates, preferring deliberate changes. Chezmoi stores real config files in a git repo and applies them to the home directory, running scripts and handling machine-specific settings. This setup simplifies bootstrapping new Macs and keeps agent skills and configs consistent across devices.

tutorials.title: Gateway pattern to invoke external dependencies
tutorials.author: Redowan Delowar
tutorials.summary: The Gateway pattern helps separate business logic from external service calls by using interfaces. In Go, the consumer defines the interface, allowing easy testing with mocks. This design keeps the service and external dependencies independent and testable.

tutorials.title: Starting Systems Programming, Pt 1: Programmers Write Programs
tutorials.author: Efron Licht
tutorials.summary: The article explores systems programming by examining what a program is and how to interact with its data. It includes practical exercises using Go programs and bash scripts to read, write, and manipulate binary data. The goal is to understand programming fundamentals and build tools to analyze programs effectively.

tutorials.title: How Servers Work: A Hands-On Introduction to TCP Sockets
tutorials.author: Ivan Velichko
tutorials.summary: A TCP server communicates by sending and receiving data over network connections called sockets. TCP ensures reliable and ordered delivery of data between clients and servers using ports and connections. The article explains how to build a simple TCP server and client in Python using sockets to send and receive data.

tutorials.title: How to build a remarkable command palette
tutorials.author: Tim Boucher
tutorials.summary: A command palette is a user interface tool that allows quick access to various commands, making it easier for users to discover features. To build an effective command palette, ensure it is available everywhere, centralizes all commands, and offers flexibility in command matching. By following these principles, you can create a powerful and user-friendly command palette that enhances productivity.

tutorials.title: Unlocking Reading Insights: A Guide to Data Analysis with Claude and Readwise
tutorials.author: Alexander Opalic
tutorials.summary: This blog post explains how to use Claude.ai's CSV analysis feature with Readwise data for better insights. It highlights the importance of crafting specific prompts to extract meaningful information and create visualizations. The tutorial also touches on the technical aspects of how Claude processes and analyzes the data.

tutorials.title: Issuing TLS Certificates in Go
tutorials.author: Software Engineering & Personal Thoughts
tutorials.summary: This guide explains how to create TLS certificates in Go, starting with self-signed certificates and building a chain of trust using root and intermediate Certificate Authorities. It shows how to generate keys, create certificate templates, and sign certificates, including those from Certificate Signing Requests (CSRs). The process helps secure communication by ensuring certificates are trusted and valid for their intended use.

tutorials.title: USB for Software Developers
tutorials.author: WerWolv
tutorials.summary: Writing a USB driver is similar to writing a network application and does not require kernel code. USB devices identify themselves using standard descriptors, which the host reads to understand the device and its capabilities. Developers can communicate with devices through specific endpoints using simple commands, as shown in the Fastboot example.

tutorials.title: Why Good Developers Write Bad Unit Tests
tutorials.author: Michael Lynch
tutorials.summary: Software developers often write bad unit tests by blindly applying production code rules to test code, leading to unnecessary complexity. Good unit tests should be simple, clear, and self-contained, enabling easy understanding and issue diagnosis without excessive abstraction. Naming tests effectively and avoiding unnecessary constants can help improve the quality of unit tests.

tutorials.title: I Rebuilt Traceroute in Rust and It Was Simpler Than I Expected
tutorials.author: Stonecharioteer on Tech
tutorials.summary: The author rebuilt the network tool traceroute using the Rust programming language and found it simpler than expected. Traceroute works by sending packets with increasing TTL values that expire at each hop, causing routers to send back ICMP messages revealing their addresses. The article explains this process and shows a basic Rust implementation that listens for these ICMP replies to map the path to a target IP.

tutorials.title: Donut math: how donut.c works
tutorials.author: a1k0n.net
tutorials.summary: The code draws a spinning 3D donut using ASCII characters by projecting 3D points onto a 2D screen with math involving rotations and perspective. It calculates the brightness of each point based on lighting and chooses characters to show shading. This creates a cool visual effect of a rotating donut made from simple text symbols.

tutorials.title: Starting Systems Programming 02: Your program and the outside world
tutorials.author: eblog: software articles by efron licht
tutorials.summary: The text explains how programs interact with the operating system using system calls, particularly focusing on command-line arguments and file operations. It describes writing simple programs that utilize syscalls for tasks like printing and reading files. The article also introduces creating a basic shell that executes commands entered by the user.

tutorials.title: ASCII characters are not pixels: a deep dive into ASCII rendering
tutorials.author: alexharri.com
tutorials.summary: ASCII characters are not simple pixels; their shapes affect how images appear when rendered as ASCII art. By using multiple sampling points and enhancing contrast, we can create sharper and clearer ASCII images. These techniques improve readability and capture the shape of characters better than traditional pixel-based methods.

fundamentals.title: Why TypeScript 7.0 Was Rewritten in Go — And What It Means for Your Dev Stack
fundamentals.author: spf13
fundamentals.summary: TypeScript 7.0 was rewritten in Go to make builds much faster and code easier to maintain. Go’s simplicity, fast compile times, and strong typing help catch errors early and support long-running, complex systems. For AI-driven development, Go is the best choice for building reliable infrastructure, while Python and Rust serve other important roles.

fundamentals.title: Agentic Autonomy Levels
fundamentals.author: Addy Osmani
fundamentals.summary: Agentic autonomy levels guide how much freedom AI agents have, balancing risk and control. Lower levels need human oversight, while higher levels let agents work independently or in parallel with evidence to verify success. The best approach matches autonomy to task risk and verification, ensuring safe and effective AI use.

fundamentals.title: Software Development in 2026
fundamentals.author: Aleksei Matiushkin
fundamentals.summary: Large language models help developers by writing documentation and tests but cannot replace expert coding for complex tasks. Using these models well requires understanding how they work and breaking problems into clear, simple steps. Many people overestimate their abilities, so careful supervision and knowledge remain essential.

fundamentals.title: Prompt caching: 10x cheaper LLM tokens, but how?
fundamentals.author: ngrok
fundamentals.summary: Prompt caching stores and reuses parts of LLM requests to avoid repeating work. This cuts token usage and cost by up to tenfold. It requires tracking inputs, outputs, and cache validity to stay correct.

fundamentals.author: arxiv.org
fundamentals.summary: Software development now faces three kinds of debt: technical debt (messy code), cognitive debt (lost shared understanding), and intent debt (unclear goals). Generative AI speeds up coding but can worsen cognitive and intent debt by reducing team understanding and clarity. To stay healthy, software teams must focus as much on clear intent and shared knowledge as on code quality.

fundamentals.title: Why Elixir is the best language for AI
fundamentals.author: José Valim
fundamentals.summary: Elixir is the best language for AI because it is easy to understand, stable, and well-documented. Its features like immutability and clear data flow help both humans and AI models reason about code. Also, Elixir’s fast feedback, low complexity, and introspection tools make coding and debugging quicker and simpler.

fundamentals.title: The Phoenix Primitives
fundamentals.author: The Phoenix Architecture
fundamentals.summary: In regenerative software, code is not maintained but recreated from precise specifications, making the specification the true source of truth. The key architectural focus shifts from internal code structure to defining clear boundaries between independently regenerable modules. Provenance replaces traditional version control by tracking the causes and effects of changes, enabling better understanding and management of system evolution.

fundamentals.title: What Async Promised and What it Delivered
fundamentals.author: Causality
fundamentals.summary: Async programming evolved from callbacks to promises to async/await, each improving code readability but adding new challenges. Async/await makes asynchronous code look sequential, which helps for simple tasks but hides complexity in larger programs. Overall, these advances helped developers write async code easier but introduced new bugs and harder maintenance in big projects.

fundamentals.title: Why German Strings are Everywhere
fundamentals.author: cedardb.com
fundamentals.summary:
German Strings use a single 128-bit layout to represent any string.  
Strings of 12 or fewer characters are stored inline; longer strings store a length, a pointer, and a four-character prefix for fast checks.  
They are immutable and support persistent, transient, and temporary storage classes to cut copies and speed reads, but appending is costly and lifetimes must be managed.

fundamentals.title: Starting Systems Programming 03: Execution Counts: Software Performance & Measurement
fundamentals.author: eblog: software articles by efron licht
fundamentals.summary: Software performance is best improved by focusing on memory and in-process operations early in design. Benchmarks and profiling help identify bottlenecks and optimize tasks like memory allocation. Using techniques like pooling reduces runtime and memory use, saving costs and improving efficiency.

fundamentals.title: What every programmer absolutely, positively needs to know about encodings and character sets to work with text
fundamentals.author: kunststube.net
fundamentals.summary: To work with text in computers, understanding encodings and character sets is essential. Unicode is a standard that unifies different encoding schemes, like UTF-8 and UTF-16, which represent characters using varying numbers of bits. It's important to specify the encoding used for text, as incorrect handling can lead to unreadable documents.

fundamentals.title: Migrating from Go to Rust
fundamentals.author: Matthias Endler
fundamentals.summary: Go and Rust both offer strong concurrency and performance, but Rust has stricter safety checks and a more powerful type system. Rust’s generics and traits provide better code reuse and fewer runtime errors, though compile times are slower and the learning curve is steeper. Moving from Go to Rust means trading simplicity and fast builds for safety, expressiveness, and fewer runtime bugs.

fundamentals.title: How The Heck Does Shazam Work?
fundamentals.author: Shri Khalpada
fundamentals.summary: Shazam works by turning sounds into simple fingerprints that help identify songs. Most services send audio to a server with a huge database to find matches. Newer apps can do this on your phone using smaller databases and smart algorithms.

fundamentals.author: Ibrahim Diallo
fundamentals.summary: Image format choices have a huge impact on site speed and bandwidth. Use JPEG for photos, PNG for simple graphics and transparency, and SVG for scalable icons and logos. React guides often skip this, so developers unknowingly bloat apps and hurt user experience.

timely.title: Agentic Code Review
timely.author: Addy Osmani
timely.summary: AI generates code faster but creates more issues, making review the slowest and costliest part of development. Human reviewers must spend more time understanding AI-written code since it lacks clear reasoning. Teams should focus on using AI to handle simple checks and save human effort for critical reviews where mistakes matter most.

timely.title: Why TypeScript 7.0 Was Rewritten in Go — And What It Means for Your Dev Stack
timely.author: spf13

Go’s simplicity, fast compile times, and strong typing help catch errors early and support long-running, complex systems. For AI-driven development, Go is the best choice for building reliable infrastructure, while Python and Rust serve other important roles.

timely.title: Vibe Coding Is Dangerous, Agentic Engineering Isn't—Wes McKinney
timely.author: Simon Späti
timely.summary: Wes McKinney uses careful planning and AI agents to write and review code, avoiding "vibe coding." He builds tools that help maintain projects and improve AI-driven development. Wes believes strong specs and engineering skills are key for successful agentic engineering in the future.

timely.title: An AI agent coding skeptic tries AI agent coding, in excessive detail
timely.author: Max Woolf's Blog
timely.summary: The author tested AI coding agents and found them surprisingly good at writing and optimizing Rust and Python code. These agents created fast, efficient machine learning tools that rival existing libraries. The author encourages others to try modern agents with clear coding guidelines for better results.

timely.title: LLMs and performative productivity
timely.author: Josh Collinsworth
timely.summary: AI tools like large language models (LLMs) often make developers feel more productive, but studies show they may actually slow work and reduce skill growth. Productivity gains are mostly seen in simple tasks, while complex projects can suffer from lower code quality and more maintenance. True productivity is hard to measure and requires careful thought, not just faster or more code output.

timely.title: / Isometric NYC
timely.author: cannoneyed.com
timely.summary: The author used AI agents to help build a pixel art map of NYC with very little coding. Image generation models still struggle with mistakes and automation is hard. Despite challenges, AI tools make large creative projects possible and inspire hope for the future.

timely.title: Shipping at Inference-Speed
timely.author: Peter Steinberger
timely.summary: AI models like Codex and GPT-5.2 now write working code fast, so the author spends more time thinking than typing. He uses agents and queues to iterate quickly and prefers simple, agent-friendly codebases. Improved models reduced the need for tools he built, letting him build and refactor more often.

timely.title: Software Engineering in the Age of AI
timely.author: Andrew Diamond
timely.summary: AI has changed software development by writing most code, while humans now mainly review and guide it. This shift makes developers less creative and risks losing deep knowledge needed for complex problems. In the long run, relying on AI may weaken the skills and understanding that build truly innovative software.

timely.title: Why AI hasn’t replaced software engineers, and won’t
timely.author: Arvind Narayanan
timely.summary: AI has not replaced software engineers because it mainly helps with routine coding, while humans still handle key decisions and quality checks. Stories of AI causing mass layoffs are often misleading and used to mask other business reasons. Instead of reducing jobs, AI is changing how software is made and may even increase the demand for engineers.

timely.author: @johnallsopp
timely.summary: Experienced software engineers resist AI-assisted coding because it challenges their long-held beliefs and skills. This resistance follows a pattern of paradigm shifts described by Thomas Kuhn, where new ideas disrupt old frameworks. Despite skepticism, AI tools are proving to boost productivity and change software development fundamentally.

timely.title: The Next Thing Will Not Be Big
timely.author: Glyph Lefkowitz
timely.summary:
Technology’s fastest, life-changing waves (like the Internet and smartphones) were a rare anomaly and are unlikely to repeat.  
Future tech will keep advancing, but mostly in smaller, niche ways that won’t remake society or create another Apple/Google.  
Open source maintainers should focus on practical, small- to medium-scale projects that serve real users and resist “scale creep.”

timely.title: Adapting to AI: Reflections on Productivity
timely.author: Colin Breck
timely.summary: In 2025, AI greatly boosted productivity by helping with coding and problem-solving, acting like a tireless partner. Most software engineers have not yet fully adapted to AI’s rapid changes and potential. The way people work in software is changing fast, and it will take years to find new, effective patterns.

timely.summary: AI companies face challenges making profits by just selling model inference because it is a commodity with little differentiation. To succeed, they must move up the stack by offering integrated services and creating switching costs like traditional enterprise software firms. This shift raises important questions about competition, innovation, and who will benefit from AI’s economic impact.

timely.title: Celebrating 50 years of Microsoft | Bill Gates
timely.author: Bill Gates
timely.summary: Bill Gates reflects on the 50th anniversary of Microsoft, starting with the creation of Altair BASIC in 1975. He shares his pride in how this early code led to a revolution in computing and the company's immense success. Gates also acknowledges the influential teachers who helped shape his journey into the world of technology.

timely.title: Twenty Five Years of Computing
timely.author: susam.net
timely.summary: The author has over 25 years of experience in software development, starting from university days. Early challenges and learning moments helped them grow into a skilled engineer. They value professionalism, continuous learning, and kindness in their career.

timely.title: The Software Industrial Revolution
timely.author: cannoneyed.com
timely.summary: The Software Industrial Revolution will make software much cheaper and easier to create. This change will boost demand for software and transform many industries beyond tech. As software becomes abundant, it will drive faster innovation and reshape the global economy.

timely.title: Goodbye, forever, probably.
timely.author: whitep4nth3r.com
timely.summary: The author has retired from developer relations after years of burnout and industry changes. They no longer find value in teaching tech as the field shifts with AI and new trends. Now, they look forward to a quieter role as a staff engineer and rebuilding themselves away from the spotlight.

timely.title: “Conviction Collapse” and the End of Software as We Know It
timely.author: Tim O’Reilly
timely.summary: Software is no longer a fixed product but a flexible process that evolves through ongoing learning and creativity. AI and agentic coding let people build, adapt, and improve software like art or music. Success now depends on play, social interaction, and discovering new ways to create, not just on money or technology.

timely.title: AI vs. human illustrators? AI + human illustrators!
timely.author: Travis Turner (richardturner@evilmartians.com)
timely.summary: Evil Martians tried using AI alone to create blog illustrations but found many problems with quality and consistency. They now use a mix of AI and human illustrators, where AI does most work and humans finish the details. This hybrid approach saves time, lowers costs, and improves the final images.

timely.title: 2025 in review
timely.author: Kevin Renskers
timely.summary: 2025 was a productive year: I wrote 38 articles, grew site traffic a lot, and released several open-source Django projects. In November my girlfriend and her daughter were in a serious car crash, so I’ve been caring for them and our dog. I started using AI cautiously, did freelance work for Sound Radix, and enjoyed trips, concerts, and games.

timely.title: My audio interface has ssh enabled by default
timely.author: hhh.hn
timely.summary: The author bought a Rodecaster Duo for better audio during gaming and found it easy to use. They discovered the device has SSH enabled by default and allows easy firmware updates without signature checks. The author created custom firmware to access the device via SSH and reported the security concern to Rode.

timely.title: The University In The AI Era
timely.author: htmx.org
timely.summary: The author suggests combining computer science with other majors to help more students learn useful tech skills. They also propose using special computer labs and oral exams to better check students’ true abilities. These changes can keep universities important even as AI grows and changes how we learn.

timely.title: Bypassing DPI with eBPF sock_ops
timely.author: Bora Tanrikulu
timely.summary: eBPF sock_ops, fake TLS packets, and why every platform needs a different hack
